title: Business case roles and links to the principles
blurb: Say who owns, prepares and supports the business case, and how the business case practice applies each of the seven principles.
question: The senior user says that, as the person who will use the new system, she should own the business case. Is she right, and which role is accountable for it?

teach.h: Who owns the argument, who owns the gains
teach.body: Formally: the executive secures funding for the project and is accountable for the business case and continued business justification. The senior user is accountable for specifying the benefits, and is responsible for demonstrating that forecast benefits are on track and, after closure, for their continued realization. The senior supplier represents the suppliers, commits their resources and is accountable for the quality and technical integrity of what they deliver. In plain English: the executive owns the case, the users own the gains, the suppliers own the build.

teach.body: Ensure continued business justification applies to every party: suppliers need their own balance of benefits, costs and risks to justify taking part, separate from the customer's business case. The senior supplier typically confirms that the products can be delivered within the expected cost and time, which feeds the customer's case, while being accountable for the quality and technical integrity of the supplier's products.

teach.caption: DVA = desirable, viable, achievable. The first three links are the ones exam questions use most.

teach.body: Fernhill Community Transport, a charity, is replacing its phone-based booking with an online system. Chief executive Helen Ward is the executive: she secures grant funding and is accountable for the business case. Operations manager Kwame Asante, the senior user, specifies the benefit of 30% fewer missed pickups and will realize it after go-live. Sofia Petrov, director of the software firm, is senior supplier. Project manager Ravi Mehta prepares the full business case, consulting project assurance, and draws on lessons from a similar charity's project.

teach.text: Classic trap: giving the business case to the senior user. The executive is accountable for the business case and funding; the senior user specifies and realizes the benefits. Second trap: the project manager prepares and maintains the business case (responsible) but is not accountable for it. Third: checking justification at stage boundaries is the manage by stages link, not focus on products.

items: Executive: accountable for the business case; secures funding.
Senior user: specifies benefits, shows they are on track, realizes them after closure.
Senior supplier: supplier resources, quality and technical integrity; suppliers need their own justification.
Prepare the full business case: executive A, project manager R, project assurance C.
Principle links: create and maintain the case; stage boundaries check justification; products lead to benefits.

summary: You can now say who is accountable for the business case, who specifies and realizes benefits, and what the senior supplier and project manager contribute. You can also match business case actions to the principles they apply, especially continued business justification, manage by stages and focus on products.

A.q: Which role is accountable for the business case?
A.why: The executive secures funding and is accountable for the business case and continued business justification.

whyNot.0: The senior user specifies and realizes the benefits but does not own the business case.
whyNot.1: The project manager prepares and maintains it on the executive's behalf.
whyNot.3: The senior supplier represents supplier interests and the quality of supplier products.

A.q: Which role is accountable for specifying the benefits and demonstrating to the business that the forecast benefits are on track?
A.why: The senior user is accountable for the specification of benefits and demonstrates that forecast benefits are on track to being realized.

whyNot.0: The executive owns the business case and funding, not the specification of benefits.
whyNot.2: Project assurance gives independent assurance; it does not specify benefits.
whyNot.3: The project manager maintains the business case but does not specify the benefits.

A.q: The business case practice ensures that decisions made at stage boundaries are checked for continued business justification. Which principle does this support?
A.why: Checking decisions at stage boundaries for continued business justification is the business case link to manage by stages (tab 5.2).

whyNot.0: Manage by exception relates to tolerances and escalation.
whyNot.1: Focus on products relates to products leading to outcomes and benefits.
whyNot.2: Learn from experience relates to using lessons from previous projects.

B.q:
Which two statements about business case roles are correct?
1. The executive secures funding for the project.
2. The project manager is accountable for the full business case.
3. The senior user has an ongoing commitment to benefits realization after closure.
4. Project assurance is accountable for approving the business case.
B.why: The executive secures funding (1), and the senior user is responsible for continued benefits realization after the project has closed (3).

whyNot.0: Both are false: the project manager is responsible, not accountable, and assurance is consulted.
whyNot.2: Statement 2 is false: the executive is accountable; the project manager is responsible.
whyNot.3: Statement 4 is false: project assurance is consulted; it does not approve the business case.

B.q: Which principle does the business case practice support by ensuring that the products produced can lead to the required outcomes and benefits?
B.why: Ensuring products can lead to the required outcomes and benefits is the business case link to focus on products (tab 5.2).

whyNot.1: Manage by stages links to checking justification at stage boundaries.
whyNot.2: Tailoring links to adapting the format and detail of the business case.
whyNot.3: Manage by exception links to benefits tolerance and escalation.

B.q: In the 'prepare the full business case' activity, which role is responsible for the work?
B.why: The project manager is responsible for preparing the full business case; the executive is accountable and project assurance is consulted.

whyNot.0: The executive is accountable, not responsible.
whyNot.2: The business layer is not involved in this activity.

C.q: In 'prepare the full business case', which roles are accountable and responsible?
options: Senior user accountable; project manager responsible
C.why: Official RACI: the executive is accountable, the project manager responsible, project assurance consulted.

whyNot.2: The senior user specifies benefits but is not accountable for the business case.
whyNot.3: Project assurance is consulted, not responsible for the work.

C.q: A supplier's director asks why her firm needs its own view of the project's costs, benefits and risks. Which statement is correct?
options: The customer's business case covers the supplier's interests
The supplier's justification is held by the executive
Each party, suppliers included, needs its own justification
The senior supplier owns the customer's business case
C.why: All parties, including suppliers, need a balance of benefits, costs and risks to justify their own involvement (manual 2.1).

whyNot.0: The customer's business case justifies the customer's investment, not the supplier's.
whyNot.1: The executive owns the customer's business case, not the supplier's justification.
whyNot.3: The executive, not the senior supplier, is accountable for the business case.

C.q: A forecast shows benefits will fall outside the agreed benefits tolerance, so the deviation is escalated. Which principle is being applied, and where is that tolerance documented?
options: Manage by stages; benefits management approach
Manage by exception; project product description
Focus on products; sustainability management approach
Manage by exception; benefits management approach
C.why: Setting tolerances and escalating forecast breaches is manage by exception; benefits tolerance is documented in the benefits management approach.

whyNot.0: The product is right, but escalating a tolerance breach is manage by exception, not manage by stages.
whyNot.1: The principle is right, but the project product description holds quality expectations, not benefits tolerance.
whyNot.2: Neither fits: tolerance escalation is manage by exception, and benefits tolerance is not in the sustainability approach.

reteach.title: Buying a minibus for a sports club
reteach.question: A sports club buys a minibus. Who should own the decision to spend the money, who should prove it was worth it, and who supplies it?

blocks.body: The club treasurer raises the money and answers for the decision: that is the executive and the business case. The team coach says what the club will gain (more away fixtures, fewer cancelled matches) and makes sure it happens long after the purchase: that is the senior user and the benefits. The dealer commits the vehicle and stands behind its quality, with its own reasons for the sale: that is the senior supplier.

blocks.text: The person who uses the result (senior user) does not own the business case. The executive does.

explain.body: Single point of accountability. Secures funding and is accountable for the business case and continued business justification.

test.q: Which responsibility belongs to the executive?
test.why: The executive secures funding for the project and is accountable for the business case.

whyNot.1: Specifying benefits is the senior user's responsibility.
whyNot.2: Committing supplier resources is the senior supplier's responsibility.
whyNot.3: Maintaining registers is typically done by project support.

explain.body: Specifies the benefits, demonstrates that forecast benefits are on track, and has an ongoing commitment to realizing them after the project closes.

test.q: Who has an ongoing commitment to realizing benefits after the project closes?
test.why: The senior user is responsible for handover, adoption and continued realization of benefits after closure.

whyNot.0: The project manager's role ends with the project.
whyNot.2: Team managers deliver products during the project.
whyNot.3: The senior supplier represents supplier interests, not the realization of user benefits.

explain.body: Represents the suppliers, commits supplier people and resources, and is accountable for the quality of supplier products and technical integrity.

test.q: Which is a senior supplier responsibility?
test.why: The senior supplier is accountable for the quality of products delivered by suppliers and the project's technical integrity.

whyNot.0: Securing funding is the executive's responsibility.
whyNot.1: Specifying benefits is the senior user's responsibility.
whyNot.3: The executive is accountable for the business case, which the board approves.

explain.body: Ensure continued business justification is applied by creating and maintaining a business case to assess whether the project is, and remains, desirable, viable and achievable.

test.q: Which principle is applied by creating and maintaining a business case to assess whether the project remains desirable, viable and achievable?
test.why: Creating and maintaining a business case to assess desirability, viability and achievability is the business case link to ensure continued business justification (tab 5.2).

whyNot.1: The roles link is about who owns the business case and who specifies the benefits.
whyNot.2: Tailoring links to adapting the format and detail of the business case.
whyNot.3: Manage by stages links to checking justification at stage boundaries.
